title: Coroutines, UniTask and cancellation
sub: Who calls MoveNext, what stops a coroutine and an async method, destroyCancellationToken
cards/0/body:
A coroutine is a method that returns IEnumerator and contains yield return. As with async (u3.l2), the compiler turns it into a state machine: each MoveNext call runs the code up to the next yield and stops.

  • 1. StartCoroutine(Blink()) runs the first MoveNext immediately and stores the enumerator under this MonoBehaviour.
  • 2. Whatever yield returned tells Unity when to call MoveNext again: null means the next frame, new WaitForSeconds(0.5f) means half a second later.
  • 3. MoveNext returned false: the coroutine is finished.

Since Unity calls MoveNext itself, Unity decides when to stop. A coroutine stops when its object is destroyed, when the object is deactivated with gameObject.SetActive(false), and on StopCoroutine. But enabled = false on the script itself doesn't stop it: only Update and the script's other events are switched off.

Limitations. You can't return a value: yield hands instructions to Unity, not a result. yield return can't sit inside a try that has a catch (compile error CS1626). An exception in a coroutine is merely logged to the console by Unity and stops it; whoever started it never finds out.
cards/1/q: The Blink coroutine was started in Start. Then the script was switched off: enabled = false. What happens to the blinking?
cards/1/options/0: It keeps going: disabling the component doesn't stop a coroutine
cards/1/options/2: It pauses and resumes on enabled = true
cards/1/explain: A coroutine is stopped by destroying the object, SetActive(false) and StopCoroutine. enabled = false only switches off Update and the script's other events.
cards/2/body:
For an async method, MoveNext isn't called by Unity but by whatever completed the wait: an Awaitable, a task, a pool thread. None of them know anything about the GameObject. So destroying the object doesn't stop an async method. Step by step (numbers match the code):

  • 1. While the method waits for 5 seconds, the object is destroyed: Destroy, a scene change.
  • 2. The wait knows nothing about the object: it completes and calls MoveNext.
  • 3. Unity overrides == for its objects: a destroyed object "equals null" even though the C# reference is alive.
  • 4. Touching the engine side (transform, components) throws MissingReferenceException. The script's ordinary C# fields can still be read.

The editor has one more case: you exit Play Mode, the scene is unloaded, and running Tasks keep working until they finish.
cards/3/q: The object is destroyed during await Awaitable.WaitForSecondsAsync(5). What happens to an async method without a cancellation token?
cards/3/options/0: It keeps running and fails with MissingReferenceException on the first access to transform
cards/3/options/2: Unity cancels it automatically when the object is destroyed
cards/3/explain: An async method's MoveNext is called by the completed wait, not by Unity. You have to stop it explicitly, with a cancellation token.
cards/4/body:
Since Unity 2022.2 every MonoBehaviour has a destroyCancellationToken: Unity cancels it when this MonoBehaviour is destroyed (Destroy, a scene unload). Pass it into your waits:

  • 1. The object is destroyed during WaitForSecondsAsync(2f, ct).
  • 2. The token is cancelled: the wait is aborted, and await throws OperationCanceledException (u2.l5).
  • 3. The lines after await don't run; the method ends in the Canceled state.
  • 4. Cleanup goes in finally: it runs on cancellation too. Just don't touch this object's Unity API there: the object is gone.

The token is cancelled only on destruction: SetActive(false) and enabled = false leave it alone, so a deactivated object keeps patrolling. And it only works where you passed it: an await without the token won't notice the cancellation. Unity recommends caching the token in a variable up front, while the object is alive.
cards/5/q: Stop the patrol together with the object
cards/5/explain: CancellationToken.None is never cancelled, and gameObject and this aren't tokens.
cards/6/q: Unity 6. PatrolAsync is running with destroyCancellationToken. The object is deactivated: gameObject.SetActive(false). What happens?
cards/6/options/0: The patrol continues: the token is cancelled only when the object is destroyed
cards/6/options/1: The patrol stops, just as a coroutine would
cards/6/options/2: await throws OperationCanceledException, and on SetActive(true) the patrol resumes where it left off
cards/6/explain: SetActive(false) stops coroutines, but it doesn't cancel destroyCancellationToken. If you need to stop on deactivation, pass your own token and call Cancel on its CancellationTokenSource in the same place where you deactivate the object.
cards/7/body:
UniTask is a free library by Cysharp (installed as a package from GitHub or OpenUPM). It appeared long before Awaitable, and here's how it works:

  • UniTask and UniTask<T> are structs, like ValueTask (u3.l3): almost no allocations, and the same rule: one UniTask is awaited once. Need more: .Preserve().
  • UniTask continuations don't go through a SynchronizationContext: the library plugs its own points into Unity's player loop and resumes wherever you asked: UniTask.Yield(PlayerLoopTiming.Update), UniTask.NextFrame(), UniTask.Delay(ms).
  • Wrappers for Unity's asynchronous API (AsyncOperation, UnityWebRequest, uGUI events) with cancellation via .WithCancellation(ct).
  • It has UniTask.WhenAll and UniTask.WhenAny; Awaitable has no combinators of its own.

When to use which: in Unity 6 the built-in Awaitable is enough for simple code. UniTask is chosen for its rich API and combinators, and in projects on Unity before 2023.1 because Awaitable doesn't exist there.
cards/8/title: Coroutine, Awaitable, UniTask: what stops what
cards/8/body:
The same patrol written three ways (code below), and who stops it:

  • Destroy: a coroutine stops on its own; Awaitable and UniTask only if destroyCancellationToken was passed into the waits.
  • SetActive(false): a coroutine stops; Awaitable and UniTask don't, even with destroyCancellationToken.
  • enabled = false: stops none of them.
  • Returning a result: a coroutine can't; Awaitable<T> and UniTask<T> can.
  • An exception: a coroutine only logs it to the console; async puts it into the task, for whoever awaits it (u2.l3).

Unity stops a coroutine because it calls the coroutine's MoveNext itself. Only a token stops async methods, because their MoveNext is called by the completed wait.
cards/9/q: Unity 6. You need to download JSON from a server, return the parsed object to the game, and not crash if the window with this script was closed (the object destroyed). What fits?
cards/9/options/0: async Awaitable<T> or UniTask<T>, with destroyCancellationToken passed into the waits
cards/9/options/2: An async void method without a token that writes the result into a field
cards/9/explain: The result and exceptions come through await, cancellation on destruction comes from the token. .Result would freeze the main thread, and async void without a token keeps running after destruction and fails when it touches the object.
cards/10/q: Match each tool to what it is
cards/10/pairs/2/1: A library: a struct, continuations in the player loop
cards/10/pairs/3/1: Cancelled when the object is destroyed
cards/11/q: What's true? Select all that apply.
cards/11/options/0: A coroutine stops when its MonoBehaviour is destroyed
cards/11/options/1: An async method stops on its own when the object is destroyed
cards/11/options/2: destroyCancellationToken is cancelled when the object is destroyed
cards/11/options/3: enabled = false stops the script's coroutines
cards/11/options/4: One UniTask, like one Awaitable, is awaited only once
cards/11/explain: async has to be cancelled with a token, and enabled = false doesn't stop a coroutine: it only switches off Update and the script's events.
